A Q&A session video from one of Apple's most significant events over the past 20 years has been circulating online — catch it before it gets taken down. Watch it below.

Watch it before Apple deletes it

Even if you weren't closely following Apple in 2010, you've probably heard of the "Antennagate" scandal and the hastily arranged press conference at the last minute, where Steve Jobs had to cut short his Hawaii vacation to come back and host it.

If you're learning about this for the first time, here's what happened: shortly after Apple launched the iPhone 4, users discovered that holding the phone in certain ways would cause the cellular signal to drop dramatically.

The fallout was so significant that Apple had to hastily arrange an event just a few weeks after the iPhone 4 went on sale.

At the event, Jobs explained that the signal drop issue wasn't unique to the iPhone 4, and that users could get a free case to prevent their hand from directly touching the antenna, or return the phone for a full refund.

After the event, Jobs, along with then-COO Tim Cook and Apple's Senior VP of Mac Hardware Engineering Bob Mansfield, held a Q&A session with the press.

Since then, there have been various accounts of what happened at that Q&A session, including one from John Gruber, who recalled asking a question that prompted Jobs, Cook, and Mansfield to pull unsleeved iPhone 4s out of their pockets, creating one of the most iconic photos of that era. However, the original footage of the Q&A has never been released — until now.

Earlier this week, the YouTube channel Sir Mix-A-Lot Rare Music (which appears to have no connection to the actual Sir Mix-A-Lot) uploaded the full 47-minute Q&A session footage in its entirety. Watch it below:

It's currently unknown how the video was obtained, or whether Apple will issue a copyright takedown request. But now that the footage has leaked, even if the original upload is removed, other backups will easily resurface elsewhere.

The fact that the video hasn't been taken down yet is a good sign. Still, if you want to see this little slice of Apple history for yourself, it's better to watch it sooner rather than later.

Were you already an Apple follower back during the "Antennagate" days? Let us know in the comments.
